Don't conflate the advance of technology with the abdication of any right to control our personal information. All of the big players on the internet (Google, Facebook, etc.) are trying their best to implant the idea that "it's impossible to provide a service to you unless you give us full access to your whole life". It's not impossible, it's not even hard, it's just contrary to their business model.

But that's the problem. Most of their products and services are reliant on data collection and it's not always nefarious or profit seeking. Metadata has lots of very legitimate uses aside from squeezing your customers for cash or quelling dissent.

Almost all of the information being collected by these cars is necessary for the concept of a driverless car to even be possible so it's kind of a moot point to focus on that aspect. It's makes more sense to focus on what is being done with the data and our rights as consumers to maintain at least some semblance of control over the information being collected about us. Right, that's why I said data retention is not necessarily part of the whole deal and the only real thing up for debate. These cars pretty much have to collect this data so we should focus less on the collection itself and more on what is done with it once the system is finished interpreting it.

And this is a perfect example of the bait-and-switch. Their products are reliant on your data, but there's no genuine need for that data to be uploaded to their servers. For most things (email search, personal assistant databases for example) you could store all of the personal data locally. In countries where mobile data is expensive, it would probably even be more practical than storing it all on the company's servers.

In many cases, having a lot of user data does make it easier to develop the service. I see nothing wrong with having an opt-in scheme (or even a properly advertised opt-out scheme, like Google's location tracking) so that users have a choice whether to share this data. I absolutely see a problem with companies forcing paying customers to give up their privacy.

A great example is the Pebble watch. The phone app needs access to your notifications, GPS location, call data, and so on, so that it can pipe all of this information through to the watch. What the app doesn't need to do is to transmit all of this to Pebble's servers - and yet it does just that.

There's nothing in most of these products that requires it to be implemented as a web service which stores all of your data with the service provider. They're just implemented this way as an excuse to get to your data.

Now all of that I won't argue against. Data collection is a necessary evil, data retention and sale is not. That's where Google oversteps the line. They convince you that data retention is part of the process when it's mostly just part of the profit. Most data about you could easily be expunged regularly without affecting the services you use in a meaningful way. But unfortunately, that data is simply much too valuable to be considered disposable.

That's why we localized services are best, and why people need to push to truly own their tech and software. The cloud is just other peoples computers and their EULA's generally say they own whatever you upload to them. It's exploitation that many people willfully sign up for, and many others reluctantly do just to operate normally in the modern world.
